artifacts.body: Metformin 1000 mg BID #180 (30-day supply at full adherence). Refill dates: Month 1 filled Day 0, Month 2 filled Day 47 (17 days late), Month 3 filled Day 93 (16 days late from prior fill). Pattern suggests approximately 30-35% of prescribed doses are being missed. Glipizide 5 mg daily refilled on time each month (Day 0, 30, 60).

artifacts.title: Endocrinology Follow-up Note (3 months ago)
artifacts.author: Endocrinology Clinic
artifacts.body: 18-year-old male with Type 2 DM diagnosed at age 15, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Reports fatigue, polydipsia, polyuria, intermittent blurred vision. Exam notable for mild bilateral lower extremity edema, no neuropathy on monofilament testing. Discussed importance of medication adherence and lifestyle modification. Referred for nutrition counseling. Plan: continue metformin and glipizide, recheck HbA1c in 3 months, nutrition referral placed.

objectives.text: Apply the Nutrition Care Process to complete an ADIME note and formulate an appropriate PES statement reflecting excessive carbohydrate/fat intake, inadequate fiber intake, and medication-food timing issues related to inconsistent adherence.
Identify a mismatch between patient-reported medication adherence and objective pharmacy refill evidence, and explore it non-judgmentally.

Develop practical, budget-conscious, developmentally appropriate nutrition interventions addressing fiber intake for constipation, reduction of added sugar/sugary beverages, and fat intake for dyslipidemia, without framing them as restrictive 'weight loss' advice.

Use motivational interviewing techniques (open-ended questions, affirmations, reflections, summaries) to explore ambivalence about dietary change and leverage sports performance as an internal motivator.
Sensitively assess and address constipation and bowel habits using a stepwise, trust-building approach appropriate for a shy adolescent patient.

Recognize the role of medication side effects (metformin-related GI upset) in nonadherence and counsel on nutrition strategies (timing with meals, gradual titration awareness, fiber/fluid intake) that may mitigate symptoms, while referring medication changes back to the prescriber.

mismatches.patientClaim: Wyatt initially states he takes his metformin 'pretty much every day' without issue.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows metformin refills consistently arriving 16-17 days late each month, indicating roughly 30-35% of doses are being missed over the past 3 months.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often overestimates actual medication-taking behavior; triangulating patient report with objective data (refill records) and asking non-judgmental follow-up questions can reveal barriers like GI side effects that the patient was initially reluctant to disclose.

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting an initial telehealth nutrition assessment for Wyatt Nelson, an 18-year-old male referred by his primary care physician for uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, obesity, and dyslipidemia. He has a history of T2DM since age 15. Review his available chart data before the visit. Your goals are to complete a nutrition assessment, identify a nutrition diagnosis, and begin patient-centered counseling using motivational interviewing.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Nutrition counseling referral for uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, obesity, and dyslipidemia
scenario.openingLine: Hey... yeah, my doctor said I need to talk to you about my blood sugar and stuff. It's been kind of high.
tasks: Complete a thorough diet history including meal pattern, food preferences, beverage intake, and barriers to healthy eating
Assess anthropometrics and relevant labs to inform the nutrition diagnosis
Explore medication adherence in a nonjudgmental way
Assess bowel habits as they relate to nutrition
Use motivational interviewing techniques to explore the patient's readiness for change and identify at least one patient-centered, achievable nutrition goal
Formulate a PES statement and brief ADIME note summarizing the encounter

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive carbohydrate and saturated fat intake with inadequate fiber intake related to limited nutrition-related knowledge, food preferences, and psychosocial/environmental barriers, as evidenced by elevated HbA1c (8.9%), elevated LDL (145 mg/dL) and triglycerides (180 mg/dL), low HDL (38 mg/dL), BMI 32.1 kg/m2, 24-hour recall showing high intake of refined carbohydrate/high-fat fast food and sugar-sweetened beverages, and minimal fruit/vegetable and fiber intake.
differential: Inadequate fiber intake related to food preferences and limited variety, as evidenced by constipation symptoms (BM 2-3x/week, straining, hard stools) and self-reported avoidance of fruits/vegetables
Medication nonadherence (self-management) related to GI side effects of metformin and school schedule barriers, as evidenced by pharmacy refill gaps and patient admission of skipped doses
Excessive sugar-sweetened beverage intake related to beliefs about sports performance and taste preference, as evidenced by reported near-exclusive soda intake and minimal water intake
keyFindings: Dyslipidemia: LDL 145 mg/dL, HDL 38 mg/dL, triglycerides 180 mg/dL, total cholesterol 235 mg/dL
BMI 32.1 kg/m2 (Obesity Class I) with weight trending up 15 lb over 10 months
Waist circumference 38 inches, elevated cardiometabolic risk
Diet low in fiber, fruits, and vegetables; high in refined carbohydrates, saturated fat, and added sugar
Irregular meal pattern (skipped breakfast, large dinner) and primary beverage is sugar-sweetened soda
Constipation (BM 2-3x/week, straining, hard stools, mild bloating/discomfort) likely related to low fiber and fluid intake
Metformin adherence gap identified via pharmacy refill records (~30-35% of doses missed), linked to GI side effects patient was initially reluctant to disclose
Ambivalence about lifestyle change; strong motivator is soccer performance, not weight loss framing
plan: Document ADIME note with PES statement focused on excessive refined carbohydrate/fat and inadequate fiber intake

Collaborative goal-setting using MI: identify 1-2 small, achievable changes framed around soccer performance and energy (e.g., swapping one sugary drink for water/flavored water during practice, adding one fiber source daily)

Provide practical, low-literacy, budget-conscious education on fiber sources with appealing textures (e.g., smoothies, lower-fiber fruit options, bean-based dishes) to address constipation without framing as weight-loss restriction

Discuss metformin timing/GI side effects nutrition strategies (taking with larger meal portion, gradual fiber increase, adequate hydration) and refer adherence/side-effect concerns back to prescribing physician for possible dose/formulation adjustment
Address sugary beverage intake via gradual substitution strategy; correct misconception that sugar provides sustained athletic energy, discuss appropriate sports hydration/fueling
Engage parents in meal planning support given their expressed willingness to help; provide simple, quick-prep meal ideas
Consider referral to school nurse/sports medicine and community resources (school nutrition program) for ongoing support
Schedule follow-up visit to reassess adherence, GI symptoms, and readiness to change; recheck HbA1c and lipids per PCP/endocrinology timeline
redFlags: Uncontrolled HbA1c (8.9%) with symptoms of polyuria/polydipsia/blurred vision suggesting ongoing hyperglycemia
Significant missed metformin doses increasing risk of worsening glycemic control
Dyslipidemia (LDL 145, HDL 38, TG 180) elevating cardiovascular risk at a young age
Progressive weight gain trend (195→210 lb over 10 months) despite diagnosed T2DM
Chronic constipation symptoms that, if persistent or worsening, warrant medical follow-up to rule out other causes
educationPoints: Fiber-rich foods do not need to be bland or textureless; there are many practical, appealing ways to add fiber (smoothies, oatmeal, beans in familiar dishes) that can also help with constipation
Sugary drinks give a quick energy spike followed by a crash and are not an effective fueling strategy for sports performance; water and balanced pre/post-practice snacks support better energy
Small, consistent changes (like swapping one soda for water) are more sustainable than a complete diet overhaul, especially for a busy student-athlete
Taking metformin with a full meal and gradually increasing fiber/fluid intake can help reduce GI side effects, but any medication adjustment should go through his physician
Framing changes around feeling better and performing better in soccer, rather than weight loss, may reduce self-consciousness and increase buy-in
Family involvement and simple, quick-prep recipes can address real barriers of time, cost, and cooking skill without requiring a complete lifestyle overhaul

profile.summary: An 18-year-old male high school soccer player with uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes (HbA1c 8.9%), Obesity Class I, dyslipidemia, and constipation presents for an initial telehealth nutrition assessment. The case trains dietetics students to conduct a developmentally appropriate diet history, uncover a medication-adherence mismatch via pharmacy refill records, sensitively explore constipation and body-image sensitivities, and use motivational interviewing to anchor nutrition change in the patient's intrinsic motivation (sports performance) rather than weight loss.
